bounded_proposition: Positive secondary slavery interpretation retained; P453801 gives a bounded Mesopotamian attestation involving people identified as Meluhhans, while Laursen-Steinkeller interpret them as royal donated slaves but explicitly leave their route into Babylonia unknown. Territorial designation remains under review.
required_abstention: Under review is not inconclusive or absent; external Meluhhan association/status abroad does not establish local Indus enslavement, territorial institution, recurrence or prevalence.
evidence_locus: Indus archaeological sites; Harappa tablets; P453801 from Irisagrig; specialist interpretations
inference_extent: Source-specific observations and external association only; no civilization-wide practice extent
temporal_state: Harappan-period context plus Šū-Suen year 6 month 12 record; not exact 2000 BCE
law_practice_note: Law unassessed; architecture and a Mesopotamian status record do not establish Indus legal regime.
network_territorial_note: External/network association is positive; acquisition geography and local Indus enslavement remain unknown.
historical_terms: Indus status term unknown; CDLI a-ru-a lugal = edited 'Royal offerings'; Laursen-Steinkeller give text-specific royal-donated-slave interpretation; broader a-ru-a status is not universally slave
category_mapping_note: Preserve lexical translation and text-specific social-status interpretation separately; no universal a-ru-a -> slave mapping.
language_access_limitations: English scholarship and CDLI edited text reviewed; direct Laursen-Steinkeller 2017 pp.83-84 unavailable in-session; Harappa reproduction read; no independent Sumerian or Indus reading.
geometry_unresolved_note: No sovereignty or practice polygon inferred; geometry cannot strengthen the claim.

bounded_proposition: Late Ur III evidence immediately preceding the anchor documents slavery through sale, court, household and institutional contexts across multiple southern Mesopotamian loci; broader Isin-Larsa evidence supports continuity, while exact 2000 BCE and one aggregate-wide territorial state are not claimed.
required_abstention: Do not treat the aggregate as one polity; do not convert near-anchor late-Ur-III evidence into an exact 2000 BCE observation; do not infer prevalence or dominant labor mode from archive density; do not map all dependent workers to slavery.
evidence_locus: Ur; Umma; Garshana/Umma provincial context; Nippur/private legal tradition; Irisagrig; broader southern Babylonia
inference_extent: Multiple bounded urban/legal/household contexts near the Ur III–Isin-Larsa transition; no uniform all-city-state territorial or prevalence claim.
law_practice_note: Ur-Namma legal composite shows formal slave/manumission/sale categories but is earlier normative evidence; practice is independently supported by sale records, court cases, household inventories and labor records.
network_territorial_note: Captivity and transfers are relevant source mechanisms but remain separate from territorial practice; no origin place or network automatically inherits the slavery classification.
historical_terms: arad₂; geme₂ (context-dependent worker/slave); saŋnita/sag-nita₂; saŋmunus/sag-munus; un-il₂ (serflike, legally free in Pottorf); a-ru-a/dedicated personnel; nam-ra-ak/captives
category_mapping_note: Slave status is directly/well-supported in specified sale, court and household contexts; geme₂ alone is not diagnostic, un-il₂ is not collapsed into slavery, and a-ru-a/dedicatees require source-specific mapping.
language_access_limitations: English specialist scholarship plus CDLI/ePSD2 transliterations and available translations; no independent Assyriological translation. Pottorf full PDF rate-limited; Bartash abstract only; Lafont original page anti-bot blocked but indexed reproduction read.
geometry_unresolved_note: Multiple evidence loci must not be merged into a single Sumerian slavery polygon; year-specific jurisdictions remain unresolved and geometry cannot strengthen the claim.

bounded_proposition: Hadramawt is a defensible polity frame around the anchor and slavery/property/captive relations are documented in broader South Arabian epigraphy, but accessible near-anchor Hadramitic material has not yet yielded a target-specific slave-status/practice attestation; territorial classification remains under review.
required_abstention: Under review is not absence or researched-inconclusive; do not infer absence from Raybūn-Hadrān silence, import regional Sabaic/South Arabian evidence into Hadhramaut, back-project late Hadramitic evidence, or equate generic subordinate terms with slavery.
evidence_locus: Shabwa and Raybūn for target identity/context; Raybūn-Hadrān early Hadramitic corpus; broader South Arabia only as regional category/slavery context
inference_extent: Target-specific territorial practice unresolved; broader regional evidence and later Hadramitic evidence remain outside the anchor-specific inference extent.
law_practice_note: No near-anchor Hadhramaut legal regime establishing slave status recovered; regional proprietary texts cannot substitute for Hadhramaut law/practice.
network_territorial_note: Shabwa trade connectivity is context only; network participation does not establish slave trading or territorial enslavement.
historical_terms: ʿbd; ʾdm; s¹byw/s¹bym; ʾmt/ʾmh; hgn; ʾḥrr/ʾḥrrt; translated servant
category_mapping_note: South Arabian terms show slavery/captivity and property in some contexts, but ʿbd/ʾdm/servant are not universally slave; exact Hadramitic near-anchor mappings require inscription-level recovery.
language_access_limitations: French/English publisher summaries and specialist review read; no independent Hadramitic reading. Full Hadrān/Kafas corpora, East of Aden social-structure discussion, and 2026 index/glossary not read in full.
geometry_unresolved_note: No Hadramawt practice polygon inferred; evidence loci and a polity label cannot be converted into one timeless territorial extent or strengthen the historical claim.

bounded_proposition: Cuzco around 1300 was an emerging local polity within the Killke-period transformation; later specialist scholarship reconstructs pre-Inca roots for yana-style dependency, but current evidence does not securely anchor slavery or that institution to Cuzco at 1300.
required_abstention: Under review is not absence; do not project mature Tawantinsuyu into 1300 Cuzco, equate yana/yanacona with slave, merge mita/mitimaes/camayoc/yanacona, or infer status from hierarchy, warfare or labor mobilization alone.
evidence_locus: Cuzco Valley / Killke archaeology for anchor frame; later imperial Cuzco and Cheqoq for comparison; wider pre-Inca Andes and colonial sources only as retrospective context
inference_extent: Target-specific labor status at 1300 unresolved; later imperial and retrospective evidence cannot establish anchor territorial practice.
law_practice_note: No contemporary Cuzco-1300 legal text recovered defining slavery/yana status; later Inca/colonial legal-administrative descriptions belong to different political conditions.
network_territorial_note: Later imperial relocation and labor networks are not territorial evidence for Cuzco at 1300; origin, resettlement and labor status remain separate.
category_mapping_note: Yanacona marks strong asymmetric dependency in specialist literature but is heterogeneous and not simply equivalent to slave; pre-Inca roots are retrospective reconstruction, not anchor-specific attestation.
language_access_limitations: English specialist archaeology and historical synthesis reviewed; colonial written sources not independently re-edited; no independent Quechua manuscript reading or artifact re-dating.
geometry_unresolved_note: Modern Cuzco, later imperial capital extent and broader Inca heartland are invalid automatic proxies for the 1300 node/incipient polity; geometry cannot strengthen the claim.

bounded_proposition: Around the late ninth/early tenth century, parts of the wider Viking/Rūs mobile network demonstrably engaged in capture, transport and sale of people, with near-anchor eastern evidence for explicit sale and independent western evidence for extensive captive-taking.
required_abstention: Do not treat the network as one polity or society; do not assume every captive was enslaved/sold, every port was a slave market, or connected territories shared one practice level; do not infer volume from dirhams/restraints.
evidence_locus: Eastern river routes linking Rūs, Slavic regions, Khazar and Volga Bulgar markets; western raiding zones and ship camps; Birka/Hedeby/Dublin as archaeological node context
inference_extent: Network participation and bounded capture/sale practices only; no territorial practice or population prevalence assigned to connected regions.
law_practice_note: No single Viking legal regime governs the evidence; later Scandinavian laws illuminate thraldom but cannot substitute for c.900 mobile-network practice.
network_territorial_note: Primary positive dimension is network participation; route/node evidence must not be converted into a territorial Viking slavery polygon.
historical_terms: þræll/thrall; Saqaliba; captive/prisoner; enslaved woman/concubine; Rūs
category_mapping_note: Contemporary external sources support captive/slave sale; later Old Norse thrall terminology requires source criticism; Saqaliba and Rūs are source categories, not precise modern nationalities.
language_access_limitations: Translated Arabic and western annal material plus specialist synthesis reviewed; Arabic originals and Old Norse manuscript traditions not independently edited.
geometry_unresolved_note: No giant Viking territory; future display should use route/nodal semantics or unresolved network geometry without strengthening claims.

bounded_proposition: British colonial actors used capture/removal of Andamanese people during the late-eighteenth-century contact/settlement period close to the anchor; current evidence does not establish an indigenous region-wide slavery or servile-labor institution at 1800.
required_abstention: External colonial coercion is not indigenous Andamanese slavery; ethnographic silence is not absence; do not homogenize distinct communities or backdate the 1858 penal colony/1863 Andaman Home.
evidence_locus: Late-eighteenth-century Company contact/settlement and 1790 removal to Calcutta for external coercion; Great Andaman retrospective ethnography for indigenous social context
inference_extent: External/colonial captivity supported near anchor; indigenous internal territorial slavery/servile dependency unassessed across distinct communities.
law_practice_note: Colonial practice is externally imposed; no indigenous written legal regime recovered, and later colonial penal law cannot substitute for indigenous social practice.
network_territorial_note: Removal/contact is an external event/network dimension; it must not recolor indigenous community territory as practicing the same institution.
historical_terms: kidnap/capture/confinement; convict transportation/penal labor; colonial dependency; indigenous local-group/family relations
category_mapping_note: Kidnap and confinement are coercive but not automatically chattel slavery; convict labor, colonial indigenous captivity and indigenous internal status systems remain separate.
language_access_limitations: English specialist history and digitized historical ethnography reviewed; original India Office record for 1790 removal and indigenous-language oral-history corpus not independently read.
geometry_unresolved_note: Modern archipelago boundaries are not one indigenous polity or practice extent; external removal needs event/network representation.

bounded_proposition: Near 1200, Angkor's royal-temple economy incorporated large institutionalized systems of bonded/unfree labor, with specific inscriptional contexts supporting slavery/property status and other personnel requiring broader dependency or labor labels.
required_abstention: Do not equate all temple personnel or assigned villagers with slaves, derive slave totals from K.273/K.908, infer empire-wide prevalence from Angkor's epigraphy, or map khñum universally to chattel slavery.
evidence_locus: Ta Prohm/Rajavihara and Preah Khan/Jayasri; wider Angkorian temple-inscription corpus for status comparison; linked provisioning villages as institutional network context
inference_extent: Angkor node and linked royal-temple institutions near anchor; no automatic Khmer-Empire-wide prevalence or territorial extent.
law_practice_note: Foundation/administrative inscriptions provide practice/institutional evidence but are not one comprehensive slave code; status/property context must be read claim-by-claim.
network_territorial_note: Captives/imported or ethnically labelled personnel add network dimensions but origin does not determine legal status; site evidence remains distinct from empire-wide territory.
historical_terms: khñum; khñum vraḥ; dāsa/dāsī; si; gho; tai; sanctuary/non-sanctuary personnel; captive; village obligation
category_mapping_note: Specific property/bondage contexts can support slavery; khñum/personnel labels and village obligations are heterogeneous and cannot all be normalized to slave.
language_access_limitations: English/French specialist scholarship and published editions/translations reviewed; Old Khmer/Sanskrit not independently re-edited.
geometry_unresolved_note: Temples are locatable but modern enclosures, metropolitan Angkor and Khmer imperial jurisdiction are not interchangeable practice extents.

bounded_proposition: Slavery and slave trading were established in multiple northern/central Ethiopian contexts around the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, while effective sovereignty in 1800 was fragmented and practice cannot be assumed uniform throughout the nominal empire.
required_abstention: Do not infer one homogeneous imperial practice level, back-project later borders/southern conquests, normalize tributary/servant categories to slave, or derive prevalence from traveler/market/export counts.
evidence_locus: Gondar/northern-central highlands; Tigray-Dixan-Massawa route; regional routes toward Gojjam, Sudan and Red Sea; legal tradition as context
inference_extent: Multiple regional territorial and network attestations within/around fragmented imperial frame; no uniform empire-wide extent or intensity.
law_practice_note: Fetha Nagast and older edicts recognize/regulate slave status but do not prove uniform enforcement in 1800; practice is independently supported by traveler and regional historical evidence.
network_territorial_note: Domestic practice and long-distance export routes coexist but remain separate; place of sale/export, capture location and origin identity must not be conflated.
historical_terms: barya; gabr/gaber; gäbbar/gabar; ʿamat; garad; captive; servant; tributary
category_mapping_note: Slave status is well supported in specific contexts, while gabr/gäbbar/servant/tributary terminology requires source-specific mapping and cannot be globally normalized.
language_access_limitations: English translations and specialist syntheses reviewed; Geʿez/Amharic legal manuscripts and traveler source languages not independently re-edited.
geometry_unresolved_note: Later Ethiopian imperial polygons are invalid proxies for 1800; nominal imperial institution and regional effective authority must remain distinct.
